claim_match_verification.reasoning: The claim names Harting's artificial CaCO3 concretions in egg albumen and their natural counterparts. The pinned IA scan contains Thompson's own reproductions of Harting's figures (Figs. 195-197, 201-204, 208) which are exactly those specimens, and Fig. 209 (plaice otoliths) is the natural biological counterpart Thompson explicitly equates with calcospherite structure (p. 425: 'The typical structure of a calcospherite is no other than that of a pearl, nor does it differ essentially from that of the otolith'). The measurable variables of the claim — a central nucleus, radial striation, concentric lamellae, rounded (circular) outline when isolated, polyhedral outline when crowded — are all directly digitisable from these plates. Modern specimens (Jurassic ooids; silver-chromate Liesegang rings in gelatine) are ANALOGUES and are labelled as such: ooids are natural CaCO3 coated grains with the same radial+concentric fabric; the Liesegang image is a modern replicate of the exact silver-chromate/gelatine experiment Thompson describes on p. 427.

key_quotes_ocr.text: The whole gist of the method was to bring some soluble salt of lime, such as the chloride or nitrate, into solution within a colloid medium, such as gum, gelatine or albumin; and then to precipitate it out in the form of some insoluble compound, such as the carbonate or oxalate.

after a few days, the calcium carbonate was seen to be deposited in the form of large rounded concretions, with a more or less distinct central nucleus, and with a surrounding structure at once radiate and concentric; the presence of concentric zones or lamellae, alternately dark and clear, was especially characteristic.
These round 'calcospherites' shewed a tendency to aggregate together in layers, and then to assume polyhedral, or often regularly hexagonal, outlines.
The typical structure of a calcospherite is no other than that of a pearl, nor does it differ essentially from that of the otolith of a mollusc or of a bony fish.
Where we have simple aggregates of two or three calcospherites, the resulting figure is precisely that of so many contiguous soap-bubbles.

the precipitate no longer comes down in a continuous, uniform layer, but forms a series of zones, beautifully regular, which alternate with clear interspaces of jelly, and which stand farther and farther apart, in logarithmic ratio, as they recede from the centre.
just as the ordinary rounded calcospherite is deposited about some minute point or centre of crystallisation, and as ordinary crystallisation is often started by a particle of atmospheric dust
